Our figure is the Treasury's costing (Table 6.1) shared out across households by their bus fare spending in England outside London: 10.0% of spending at £3 fares (£230m / 0.9 operator participation / £2,557m), so it is above the official figure by about the participation adjustment. Self Assessment tax for 2027-28 is paid from 31 January 2029, so the Treasury's costing (on a National Accounts basis) starts in 2028-29 (£0 in 2027-28) while the model scores each tax year's liability. Table 6.1 row 15; policy costings p. 23.

Allowance ends 5 April 2030; the Treasury's 2030-31 and 2031-32 figures (+£50m, -£15m) fall after the end, where the static model scores nothing. The policy costings (p. 63) do not explain them and assume no behavioural response (Table 6.1 row 52).

Taxpayers pay most Self Assessment tax on 2027-28 property income from 31 January 2029, so the Treasury's costing (on a National Accounts basis) has £35m in 2027-28 and about 1.5 years of liability in 2028-29 (£575m), while the model scores each tax year's liability. Table 6.1 row 61.

The rates rise from 6 April 2027. The official figure for 2026-27 (+£15m) falls before then: the OBR lists it as onshore corporation tax, which we don't model (£13m in its detailed policy table, Table 1.1, measure 62). For 2027-28 and 2028-29, the government counts the tax in its costing when taxpayers pay it, after the tax year it relates to: the OBR puts the costing's income tax at £63m in 2027-28 and £483m in 2028-29, and adds almost no Self Assessment receipts from the savings and property rate rises in 2027-28 and £1.0bn in 2028-29 (Economic and fiscal outlook, October 2026, Table 4.4). We count each tax year's liability in that year. Table 6.1 row 62.
